claim: Cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric burned along its full 29 cm length in microgravity at measured concurrent spread rates of 2.1 and 2.6 mm/s; the same samples in normal gravity also burned completely, with an accelerating spread.
condition: Samples 2-5 and 2-6, 5 cm x 29 cm, 20 cm/s concurrent air flow, ~22.1% O2, burn times 145 s and 115 s. PSI-99 lists 20 cm/s for both; the pre-flight plan (Saffire paper, Table 1) listed 30 cm/s for the second sample.
numbers: 2.1 and 2.6 mm/s over 29 cm; burn time 145 s and 115 s
citation: data/raw/PSI-99_SAFFIRE-II.csv, rows 2-5 and 2-6

claim: Silicone sheets that burned in normal gravity did not burn in microgravity: all four silicone samples show a burn length of about zero in microgravity, while in 1 g the thinnest burned completely, the 0.61 mm one burned 7.6 cm, and the opposed-flow one burned completely.
condition: Samples 2-1 to 2-4, 5 cm x 29 cm, 20 cm/s air flow, ~21.5-22.1% O2, 80 W igniter for 9.2 s. Concurrent flow at 0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm thickness; one opposed-flow sample. The 1.03 mm sample did not burn in 1 g either.
numbers: 0g burn length ~0 for all four; 1g: complete (0.27 mm), 7.6 cm at 1.2 mm/s (0.61 mm), ~0 (1.03 mm), complete at 0.6 mm/s (opposed)
citation: data/raw/PSI-99_SAFFIRE-II.csv, rows 2-1 to 2-4

claim: Reducing the air flow put flames out: 17 BASS-II runs are logged as ending in extinction while the crew stepped the flow down from 5-10 cm/s, including 6 runs that started at 20% O2 or more.
condition: PMMA rods (14 runs), thin PMMA films (2) and a PMMA slab (1); initial O2 14.8-20.9%. Counted from the 'ext' / 'extinguished' / 'out' notes in the fan and air display columns. The flow speed at extinction is mostly logged as a fan pot setting, not in cm/s.
numbers: 17 of 129 runs; 6 of them at >= 20% initial O2; O2 range 14.8-20.9%
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv (tests B14, B21, M17, O4, O6, O8a, O14, O19, P1, P5, P9, P10, P13a, P13b, P22a, P22b, P25); parsed in data/processed/bass2_structured.csv, column extinction_noted

claim: A PMMA rod kept burning in microgravity at well below normal air oxygen: a 3/8 inch clear rod ignited at 14.8% O2 and burned until the flow was reduced, while a rod of the same size at 13.6% O2 could not be ignited at any flow setting.
condition: Tests O4 and O12, same day, concurrent (upstream-ignited) flow starting at 5 cm/s. During O4 the glovebox O2 fell from 14.8% to 13.6%. Two single runs, not a statistically defined limit.
numbers: burned at 14.8% O2 (O4); no ignition at 13.6% O2 (O12)
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv, tests O4 and O12; flow geometry from the BASS-II data FAQ

claim: Gaseous fire suppressants need a higher concentration to put out a flame in microgravity than on Earth: the minimum extinguishing concentration of CO2, helium and nitrogen is higher in microgravity for all three.
condition: Methane cup-burner flames, agent mixed into standard air (Takahashi et al., 2004, as quoted in the FLEX test plan). The normal-gravity values are tests; the microgravity values are simulations. A separate cited study (Katta et al., 2004) needed more than 19.1% CO2 in microgravity against 16.4% in normal gravity.
numbers: minimum extinguishing concentration, 1g -> 0g: CO2 0.16 -> 0.19; He 0.27 -> 0.31; N2 0.26 -> 0.38 (mole fraction)
citation: FLEX Test Plan (FLEX_Test_Plan.pdf, extracted from the FLEX Research Requirements Document, Williams et al., 4 Nov 2005), PDF p. 3 (document pp. 11-12), Table 2 and section 2.3

claim: Thick PMMA burned much less in microgravity than in normal gravity: after 600 s and 900 s only about 10 cm of each sample showed visible damage, with the flame anchored at the base, whereas the 1 g samples burned completely with accelerating spread.
condition: Samples 2-8 (structured) and 2-9 (flat, 1 cm thick), 5 cm x 29 cm, 20 cm/s concurrent flow, O2 22.1 -> 21.9%, 97 W igniter for 30 s.
numbers: ~10 cm damaged of 29 cm; burn time 600 s and 900 s; regression rate 0.01-0.04 mm/s
citation: data/raw/PSI-99_SAFFIRE-II.csv, rows 2-8 and 2-9, notes 3 and 4

claim: At low oxygen a flame survives only inside a window of air speeds: the same PMMA rod was extinguished once by lowering the flow and, on the next run, blown off by raising it.
condition: 1/4 inch clear PMMA rod, sample 208m, tests O8a (15.7% O2, extinguished at low flow) and O8b (15.5% O2, blowoff at fan pot 6.0), concurrent flow. Fan pot settings are not converted to cm/s in the table.
numbers: 15.7% O2: extinction at low flow; 15.5% O2: blowoff at fan pot 6.0 (scale max 10)
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv, tests O8a and O8b; fan pot scale from the BASS-II data FAQ

claim: Every run logged as a blowoff started at reduced oxygen, and for 1/4 inch clear rods tested on one day the fan setting needed to blow the flame off dropped as oxygen dropped.
condition: 7 runs annotated 'blowoff' (thin PMMA films B18, B19; PMMA rods O7, O8b, O9, O11, O22), initial O2 15.0-17.4%. Same-day series on 26 Jun 2014: O7, O8b, O9. Absence of a blowoff note at higher O2 does not prove blowoff was attempted there.
numbers: 7 blowoff runs, all at 15.0-17.4% O2; blowoff at fan max 10 (16.0% O2), pot 6.0 (15.5%), pot 4.0 (15.0%)
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv, tests B18, B19, O7, O8b, O9, O11, O22; column blowoff_noted in data/processed/bass2_structured.csv

claim: Burning one small sample measurably fouled the sealed glovebox atmosphere: a single 3 mm PMMA slab took O2 from 22.2% to 19.0% and CO2 from 0.44% to 3.22%, and two runs drove carbon monoxide over the sensor range.
condition: Readings are for the Microgravity Science Glovebox work volume before and after each burn, not for a crew cabin. Test M5 (3 mm thick, 2 cm wide PMMA slab, two-sided burn); CO over range after tests O4 and O13b. The FAQ defines over range as > 1000 ppm. CO and CO2 carry over between runs on the same day.
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv, tests M5, O4, O13b; BASS-II data FAQ, 'CO readings'

claim: Nomex did not ignite in microgravity even when a burning PMMA strip was attached to it: the PMMA section was completely consumed and the Nomex was not ignited. Nomex did not burn in the 1 g test either.
condition: Sample 2-7, 5 cm of PMMA followed by 24 cm of Nomex, 20 cm/s concurrent flow, ~22.1% O2, 80 W igniter for 9.2 s, 140 s burn time.
numbers: 0g burn length: 5 cm (PMMA) and 0 (Nomex); 1g burn length ~0 (Nomex)
citation: data/raw/PSI-99_SAFFIRE-II.csv, row 2-7 and note 2

claim: Saffire-I burned a fabric sheet about 0.94 m by 0.4 m in microgravity, at least ten times larger in each dimension than any earlier low-gravity flame spread test; the concurrent-flow burn lasted 420 s and the opposed-flow burn 70 s.
condition: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, 20 cm/s air flow, ~21.5-21.7% O2, 182 W igniter for 8 s, aboard an uncrewed Cygnus after it left the ISS. PSI-98 gives burn times only, no spread rate.
numbers: sample 94 cm x 40.6 cm; burn time 420 s (concurrent) and 70 s (opposed)
citation: data/raw/PSI-98_SAFFIRE-I.csv, rows S1 and S2; Schoren, Ruff & Urban, 'The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status' (NTRS 20170001636), p. 2

claim: Before Saffire, microgravity fire experiments were limited to samples no larger than 10 cm, so spacecraft fire-safety design has relied on terrestrial fire standards, which NASA describes as an inherent risk that grows as missions travel farther from Earth.
condition: Statement of the knowledge gap that motivated the Saffire experiments; a qualitative assessment, not a measurement.
numbers: prior samples <= 10 cm in length and width
citation: Schoren, Ruff & Urban, 'The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status' (NTRS 20170001636), p. 1

claim: The oxygen limit at which a material burns can differ between low gravity and normal gravity, so Saffire-II chose materials whose 1 g flammability limits sit just above and just below 21% O2 to measure that difference on samples the size of NASA's standard screening test.
condition: Design rationale. The limit difference is attributed to earlier drop-tower tests (paper refs 3-5); sample size matches NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (5 cm x 29 cm).
numbers: 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm; 1 g limits near 21% O2
citation: Schoren, Ruff & Urban, 'The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status' (NTRS 20170001636), pp. 2-3; SAFFIRE-II data description (SAFFIRE-II_DoD.docx), first paragraph

claim: Saffire-I to -III did not cover exploration atmospheres: flame behaviour at elevated oxygen and lower pressure, fire detection, post-fire cleanup and water-mist suppression were all assigned to later flights (Saffire-IV to -VI) or ground tests.
condition: Table of spacecraft fire-safety objectives as of 2016. Elevated O2 with lower pressure is the atmosphere type planned for exploration vehicles and habitats, so the Saffire-I to -III results apply to roughly ISS-like air.
citation: Schoren, Ruff & Urban, 'The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status' (NTRS 20170001636), p. 5, Table 5

claim: Liquid fuel droplets self-extinguished far more often in low-oxygen atmospheres: every methanol test at 15% O2 or less ended in extinction, against about a third of tests above 22% O2; heptane followed the same direction.
condition: 274 single-droplet tests on the ISS, methanol and heptane, O2 mole fraction 0.12-0.34, pressure 0.69-3.05 atm, N2/CO2/He diluents. Raw shares by oxygen band; pressure, diluent and droplet size are not held constant.
numbers: methanol: 37/37 extinguished at x_O2 <= 0.15, 13/35 at x_O2 > 0.22; heptane: 8/11 at <= 0.15, 7/33 at > 0.22
citation: computed from data/raw/PSI-69_FLEX.csv via data/processed/flex_clean.csv, column 'Test end' = Extinction

claim: CO2, the suppressant used in the US segment of the ISS, may work less well in microgravity than expected: without buoyancy, radiation dominates heat loss, and CO2 traps that radiation near the fuel; earlier flame-spread tests suggested CO2 is less effective than helium in microgravity.
condition: Background review in the FLEX test plan. The helium comparison is from opposed-flow flame spread over thin solid fuels (Honda and Ronney, 1998) and is worded as 'seem to suggest'; measured by the minimum O2 concentration that supports combustion.
citation: FLEX Test Plan (FLEX_Test_Plan.pdf, extracted from the FLEX Research Requirements Document, Williams et al., 4 Nov 2005), PDF p. 3 (document p. 12), section 2.3

claim: Thick fuels produced far more carbon monoxide per run than thin ones: the median CO rise in the glovebox was 335 ppm for PMMA slabs and 87 ppm for PMMA rods, against 16 ppm for thin PMMA films and 19 ppm for fabric sheets.
condition: CO rise = final minus initial CSA-CP reading in the glovebox work volume, runs with both readings numeric (19 slab, 49 rod, 20 film, 27 fabric runs). Not normalised by burn time or mass burned.
numbers: median CO rise: slabs 335 ppm, rods 87 ppm, films 16 ppm, fabric 19 ppm; largest single rise 575 ppm (O15b)
citation: computed from data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv via data/processed/bass2_structured.csv, column co_rise_ppm grouped by geometry

claim: In opposed flow a 3/8 inch black PMMA rod would not stay lit at 16.4% O2 at 5, 10 or 15 cm/s, although a clear rod of the same diameter burned in concurrent flow at 14.8% O2.
condition: Test P8 (downstream-ignited, opposed flow) versus test O4 (upstream-ignited, concurrent flow). Single runs; the rods also differ in colour, so this is an observation, not a controlled comparison.
numbers: opposed: would not stay lit at 16.4% O2; concurrent: burned at 14.8% O2
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv, tests P8 and O4; flow geometry from the BASS-II data FAQ

claim: The Saffire-I to -III evidence base is small: two large samples and nine smaller ones. The authors state that a thorough evaluation would need many more samples and a wider range of materials.
condition: Limitation stated by the experiment team; applies to every Saffire result quoted in this dashboard.
numbers: 2 large samples + 9 smaller samples
citation: Schoren, Ruff & Urban, 'The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status' (NTRS 20170001636), p. 5; data/raw/PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100

claim: BASS-II was designed to test the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, given adequate ventilation, burn as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity, and to find how the worst case in a spacecraft compares with the upward-burning ground test used to screen materials.
condition: This is the hypothesis and objective stated before flight, not a result. Primary variables: ambient oxygen, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness and geometry.
citation: BASS-II Science Requirements (SRD_BASS-II.pdf), slide 9, 'BASS-II Science Overview'

claim: BASS-II gives 129 logged burns of solid fuels in microgravity across 13.6-22.2% oxygen, most of them below normal air: 102 runs started under 21% O2 and 59 under 18%.
condition: As-run test matrix, six investigators, Feb-Aug 2014 plus three runs in Feb 2016. Materials: PMMA rods, slabs, films and a spherical section (98 runs), SIBAL fabric (27), Nomex III (3), a Japan wax candle (1). The table logs settings and gas readings; it has no spread-rate or pass/fail outcome column.
numbers: 129 runs; initial O2 13.6-22.2%; 102 runs < 21% O2; 59 runs < 18% O2
citation: data/raw/PSI-25_BASS-II.csv; parsed in data/processed/bass2_structured.csv; materials per PI from the BASS-II data FAQ

claim: Two thirds of FLEX droplet flames went out on their own before the fuel was used up: 186 of 274 tests ended in extinction, 27 burned to completion and 61 ended in disruption.
condition: Methanol (157 tests) and heptane (117 tests) droplets, 1.1-4.67 mm initial diameter, March 2009 to December 2011. Liquid droplets only; says nothing about solid materials.
numbers: 186 extinction / 27 completion / 61 disruption of 274 tests
citation: data/raw/PSI-69_FLEX.csv, column 'Test end'

claim: FLEX tested carbon dioxide and helium as fire-suppressant diluents. Droplets in helium-diluted atmospheres had the highest median burning-rate constant and those in CO2 the lowest, so helium does not slow a droplet flame the way CO2 does.
condition: 123 tests with CO2 (up to 0.70 mole fraction), 50 with helium (up to 0.45), 101 with nitrogen only. Medians over tests with a measured burning-rate constant; oxygen and pressure differ between groups, so this is a raw comparison.
numbers: median K: heptane 0.65 (He), 0.56 (N2), 0.50 (CO2) mm2/s; methanol 0.585 (He), 0.44 (N2), 0.43 (CO2) mm2/s
citation: computed from data/raw/PSI-69_FLEX.csv via data/processed/flex_clean.csv, columns k_mm2_s and diluent

claim: For each fuel and atmosphere there is a limiting oxygen fraction below which a steady flame cannot exist; a total-flooding suppressant works by pushing oxygen below that limit, and FLEX was built to measure how the limit moves with pressure and suppressant.
condition: Definition and experiment objective, using a single fuel droplet as the model geometry. The relation between the limit and the minimum extinguishing concentration is given as LOI = 0.209 (1 - MEC).
numbers: LOI = 0.209 x (1 - MEC)
citation: FLEX Test Plan (FLEX_Test_Plan.pdf, extracted from the FLEX Research Requirements Document, Williams et al., 4 Nov 2005), PDF pp. 2-4 (document pp. 11-12 and 44), sections 2.2 and 5.3

claim: BASS-II oxygen and flow readings carry known instrument limits: the O2 sensor was out of calibration and corrected with a constant daily offset from the ISS reading, and the air-speed display needs about a minute to settle.
condition: Applies to every BASS-II oxygen and flow number here. Five rows of PSI-25 also hold an impossible final O2 value (tests B2, P22a, P22b, T28a, T28b), dropped in the structured table.
numbers: air display response ~1 min; science requirement +/-10% measurement accuracy; 5 of 129 rows with unusable final O2
citation: BASS-II data FAQ, 'Columns in test matrix'; BASS-II Science Requirements (SRD_BASS-II.pdf), slide 1; data/processed/bass2_structured.csv, column quality_flags

claim: In the Apollo 1 fire of 27 January 1967 a flash fire in a cabin pressurized with 100% oxygen swept through the spacecraft too fast for the crew to open the hatch; the three astronauts died of asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases, and their burns were likely survivable.
condition: Preflight test on the launch pad, hatches closed, crew in spacesuits. The review board found the pure oxygen atmosphere made the fire spread quickly; the three-piece hatch took 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions. Afterwards NASA restricted combustible materials in the spacecraft and fitted a hatch that opens in three seconds.
gravity: 1g (ground test on the launch pad, not in flight)
numbers: 100% O2 cabin; 3 crew lost; hatch 90 s to open, replaced by a 3 s hatch
citation: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance, 'Apollo 1 AS-204' (Apollo, Challenger, Columbia Lessons Learned Program), https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-1

claim: On 24 February 1997 an oxygen generator canister ignited aboard the Mir space station: a three-foot flame burned for several minutes, blocked the route to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles and filled the modules with dense smoke that took the life support system several hours to clear.
condition: Six crew aboard; solid-fuel oxygen generator in the Kvant-1 module. The crew put on oxygen masks and used three foam extinguishers; the article says the flame finally extinguished itself. No structural damage and no lasting harm to the crew. NASA calls it the worst in-orbit fire incident in the history of spaceflight.
numbers: three-foot flame, several minutes; 6 crew; 3 extinguishers; smoke cleared over several hours; generator type used over 2,500 times before without incident
citation: John Uri, '25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir', NASA Johnson Space Center, 23 Feb 2022, https://www.nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir/
